Now the important qualification, which most explanations omit: this is a definition of meaning, not a description of what happens. The executor does not materialise the whole FROM then filter it. A WHERE condition on a single table is usually pushed right down into the scan, so rows are discarded as pages are read and never exist as intermediate rows at all; a condition may even be pushed into an index so the disqualified rows are never fetched from the heap. The planner is free to do anything it likes as long as the answer matches what the logical order defines. Hold both ideas at once: the logical order tells you what a query means and therefore why the scoping rules are as they are; the plan in Node 6 tells you what it does.

Joins, and the bug everybody writes

An inner join is straightforward: for each pair of rows satisfying the ON condition, emit a combined row; unmatched rows on either side vanish.

A left join adds one rule on top: any left row that found no partner is emitted anyway, with every right-hand column set to NULL. Those NULL-extended rows are the entire reason the left join exists — they are how you answer "customers and their bookings, including customers with none."

Which sets up the most common bug in everyday SQL. Consider:

SELECT c.name, b.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.customer_id = c.id
WHERE b.status = 'confirmed';

This does not return customers with no confirmed bookings. It returns no such customer at all, because for those customers the join produced a row with b.status NULL, and NULL = 'confirmed' is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. Every NULL-extended row is discarded, and the left join has been silently converted into an inner join. This is Node 2's three-valued logic doing exactly what it said it would, in the place where it does the most damage.

The fix is to move the condition into the join predicate, where it decides which rows pair up rather than which result rows survive:

SELECT c.name, b.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN bookings b ON b.customer_id = c.id AND b.status = 'confirmed';

The general rule worth memorising: in a left join, a condition on the left table belongs in WHERE, and a condition on the right table almost always belongs in ON. In an inner join it makes no difference at all, which is why people who learned on inner joins carry the wrong habit across.

EXISTS versus IN, and the NOT IN trap. EXISTS asks whether any matching row exists and can stop at the first one. IN compares a value against a set. For the positive form the difference is usually academic, since the planner rewrites both into semi-joins. For the negative form it is not academic at all: NOT IN against a subquery that yields even one NULL returns zero rows, for every input, with no error. "x is not equal to unknown" is unknown, so the predicate is never true for anything. Use NOT EXISTS, which is immune, and which the planner handles as an anti-join. This follows directly from Node 2 and is worth recognising instantly, because the symptom — a query that returns nothing at all — looks like a data problem rather than a logic one.

Upsert, RETURNING, and pagination

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT is built directly on Node 2's mechanism, and knowing that explains its syntax. Because uniqueness is enforced by a unique index rather than by a rule, the conflict target you name — ON CONFLICT (provider_event_id) — is Postgres identifying which unique index to watch. It then performs what the implementation calls a speculative insertion: it attempts the index insert, and if a conflicting live entry is found it takes the alternative action instead, all inside one statement so there is no window for another transaction to slip between the check and the write. DO NOTHING skips; DO UPDATE SET ... updates, and inside that update the pseudo-table EXCLUDED holds the row you tried to insert, so you can write SET name = EXCLUDED.name to mean "use the new value".

Two things to know. The conflict target must correspond to an actual unique index, or Postgres cannot tell what conflict you mean. And an ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE takes a row lock on the conflicting row, so concurrent upserts of the same key serialise — correct, and worth knowing when the key is hot.

RETURNING turns a write into a read in the same round trip: INSERT INTO bookings (...) VALUES (...) RETURNING id, created_at. Without it you would insert and then run a second query to find out what you inserted, which is both a round trip you did not need and, if you get it wrong, a race. It works on UPDATE and DELETE too, and returning the deleted rows is often how you write an archive-and-remove in one statement.

Pagination. LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000 does not skip ten thousand rows cheaply — the executor must produce them and throw them away, because the only way to know which row is the ten-thousandth is to have produced the nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine before it. So the cost of a page grows with its number, and page 500 of a listing is genuinely expensive. It is also incorrect under concurrent writes: if a row is inserted while a user pages, rows shift and one gets shown twice or skipped.

Keyset pagination fixes both. Instead of a count, remember the last row's sort values and continue from there:

SELECT * FROM bookings
WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND (created_at, id) < ($2, $3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

With an index on (tenant_id, created_at DESC, id DESC) the server seeks straight to the position and reads twenty rows, so page 500 costs the same as page 1. The tuple comparison (created_at, id) < ($2, $3) is doing real work: it compares the pair lexicographically, which is exactly the ordering the composite index provides, and including id breaks ties so that rows sharing a timestamp are never skipped or repeated. The cost is that you can no longer jump to an arbitrary page number, which for an infinite-scroll or "next page" interface is not a cost at all.

In your project

Stage 2 of slotline is this node applied, and the spec deliberately puts one hard query at its centre: availability. "Which windows are free for resource X on day D" is a question about absence, and questions about absence are where most people's SQL stops, because there is no table of things that did not happen.

The shape is: use generate_series to manufacture the candidate slots for the day — a row per half-hour, say — LEFT JOIN those against existing bookings on range overlap, and keep the rows where the booking side came out NULL. Every piece of this node is in that one query: a derived table, an outer join, the NULL-extended rows being the answer rather than an inconvenience, and the discipline of putting the resource and status conditions in the ON clause rather than in WHERE — because if you put them in WHERE you will get the bug traced above and your availability query will report that nothing is ever free.

The spec's stated difficulty for Stage 2 is that the first working version will be a loop in JavaScript: fetch the bookings, build the slots in memory, filter. Write it that way if that is what comes out, then replace it, because the comparison is the lesson — the loop is imperative and pulls every booking across the network; the query is declarative, runs where the data is, and in Stage 5 becomes a single index seek.

Three smaller pieces of the stage are also this node. RETURNING id, created_at on the booking insert, so creating a booking is one round trip. The allow-list for a user-supplied ORDER BY column, which is Node 19's point arriving early: identifiers cannot be parameterised, so a sortable column name must be validated against a fixed list and never interpolated. And, later, in Stage 7, ON CONFLICT (provider_event_id) DO NOTHING on the webhook receiver — which is what makes redelivery of the same payment event harmless, and which works only because you put a unique constraint there in Stage 1.

In qbank

Drizzle's query builder is a typed way of assembling exactly these clauses: db.select().from(bookings).leftJoin(customers, eq(...)).where(...) produces the SQL above with the same semantics and the same left-join trap — a condition placed in .where() instead of in the join's eq() discards NULL-extended rows just as it does in raw SQL. The builder does not protect you from it, because it is not a bug in SQL; it is what you asked for.

The concrete exercise for closing the qbank gap is to turn on query logging for an hour of real use and read what comes out. You will be able to identify, in the log, which of your calls became a join and which became several separate statements — and that second category is the N+1 problem that Node 19 covers, visible for the first time. Drizzle's relational query API in particular tends to produce nested subqueries with JSON aggregation rather than a flat join; that is usually fine and occasionally not, and the only way to know which is to look.

The habit worth taking away is small and unglamorous: for any query you cannot picture the SQL of, log it and read it. Every ORM performance disaster is invisible until you do.

What an interviewer does with this

"What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING?" Near-universal, and the answer that separates you is the reason rather than the rule: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after, and that follows from the logical evaluation order in which GROUP BY sits between them. An aggregate cannot appear in WHERE because it does not exist yet.

Given a LEFT JOIN with a condition in WHERE: "what does this return?" A very common live-code question. The answer is that it silently behaves as an inner join, because the NULL-extended rows fail the predicate — unknown is not true. Say what the fix is (move it into ON) and why the two placements differ (one decides pairing, the other decides survival), and mention that in an inner join the placement makes no difference, which is where the wrong habit comes from.

"How would you get the most recent booking per resource?" Asked constantly. Three good answers and you should be able to give at least two: a window function, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY resource_id ORDER BY starts_at DESC) filtered to 1 in an outer query; Postgres's DISTINCT ON (resource_id) with a matching ORDER BY, which is more compact and non-standard; or a lateral join, which wins when you want the top N per group rather than one. Naming the trade-off — window functions are portable, DISTINCT ON is shorter and Postgres-only — is the part that lands.

"How do you paginate a large table?" The weak answer is LIMIT/OFFSET with no caveat. The strong one names both problems — cost grows with page number because skipped rows must still be produced, and results shift under concurrent writes so rows are duplicated or missed — then gives keyset pagination with the tuple comparison and the matching composite index, and notes the one thing you give up, which is jumping to an arbitrary page.

"Why did this query return zero rows?" If the query contains NOT IN (SELECT ...), that is the answer: one NULL in the subquery makes the predicate unknown for every candidate. Recognising it on sight is a strong signal, and the fix is NOT EXISTS.

"What happens when you send a query to Postgres?" The deeper version of Node 1's question. Parse into a tree with names and types resolved against the catalog; rewrite, which is where views are expanded and RLS policies applied; plan, which is where the cost-based decisions happen; then execute, pulling rows one at a time through a tree of nodes. Adding that LIMIT can therefore stop execution early, while a sort must consume everything before emitting anything, shows the model is real rather than recited.

sections.title: Node 4 — What a table really is: pages, tuples and the heap
sections.content:
Where this sits

Nodes 1 through 3 treated a table as an abstraction: a bag of rows you put things into and ask questions of. This node opens it and looks at the bytes, and it is the hinge of the whole topic. Every performance idea from here to the end is a consequence of what is described below. Indexes in Node 5 exist because of how a heap is laid out. The planner's cost numbers in Node 6 are counts of the unit defined here. The tuple header introduced here is where Node 8's entire concurrency model lives, and the dead tuples of Node 9 are these tuples with one field set. If you skip this node, everything after it has to be memorised; if you take it, most of it can be derived.

Every term, from absolute zero

Block or page — the fixed-size chunk Postgres reads, writes and caches. The two words mean the same thing and both are used constantly, sometimes in the same sentence. A page is 8192 bytes, which is 8 kibibytes, usually written 8 KB.

Heap — the file or files holding a table's row data. "Heap" here carries its ordinary English sense of an unordered pile, and it is literal: rows sit wherever there was space, in no meaningful order, and nothing about their arrangement reflects their contents.

Relation — from Node 1, Postgres's internal word for anything table-shaped stored in files. Tables, indexes, sequences and materialized views are all relations, which is why the built-in size functions are named pg_relation_size rather than anything with "table" in it.

Segment — Postgres splits each relation's storage into files of at most 1 GB. The first is named for the relfilenode from Node 1; the next is that number with .1 appended, then .2, and so on. This is invisible in normal use and matters only when you are looking at the directory and wondering why your table is several files.

Relation fork — each relation has, alongside its main data file, up to three small companion files with suffixes: _fsm the free space map, _vm the visibility map, and _init for unlogged tables. Note the vocabulary collision: this "fork" has nothing whatsoever to do with the process fork from Node 1. Same word, unrelated meanings.

Page header — 24 bytes at the start of every page recording, among other things, how much free space the page has and where that free space begins and ends.

Line pointer (also item identifier, ItemId) — a 4-byte entry in an array near the top of the page, pointing at where a tuple actually sits inside that page and recording its length and status. It exists so that a tuple can be moved within its page without anything outside the page having to be told, which is a property Node 9's vacuum relies on.

Tuple — from Node 1, a stored row version. In this node it becomes a concrete byte layout rather than a word.

Tuple header — 23 bytes at the front of every stored row, padded to 24, holding transaction bookkeeping rather than any of your data. Node 8 is about what those bytes mean; this node establishes that they are there and what they cost.

ctid — a tuple's physical address: a pair of numbers, the page number and the line pointer number within that page. Written like (0,1). It is a hidden system column on every table, so SELECT ctid, * FROM bookings works. It is not stable — an update can move a row and change it — so it must never be stored or used as an identifier.

Null bitmap — from Node 2: a run of bits immediately after the tuple header, one per column, marking which columns are NULL. Present only when the row has at least one NULL. Columns marked null occupy no space in the data that follows.

Alignment — the requirement that a value of a given type begins at a byte offset that is a multiple of its size. An 8-byte value must start at an offset divisible by 8. This is a hardware-derived rule that Postgres honours in its stored layout.

Padding — the wasted bytes inserted to satisfy alignment. If a 1-byte value is followed by an 8-byte one, seven bytes are thrown away between them.

varlena — short for "variable length array", Postgres's internal representation for any variable-width value such as text or numeric or jsonb. Each carries a length header: 4 bytes normally, or a compact 1 byte for values under 127 bytes, an optimisation added in version 8.3 that matters a great deal on tables of short strings.

TOAST — The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique. The mechanism that compresses large values and, if needed, moves them out of the row into a side table. The acronym is a deliberate joke and is capitalised everywhere.

Compression — here, lossless shrinking of a value's bytes so it takes less room, reversed transparently on read. Postgres has used its own algorithm, pglz, since the beginning, and since version 14 can use lz4 instead, which compresses a little less and is substantially faster.

Fillfactor — a per-table setting saying what percentage of each page inserts are allowed to fill, default 100. Lowering it deliberately leaves free space on each page, which Node 8's HOT updates need.

Free space map — a small companion file recording roughly how much usable space each page has, so an insert can find a page with room instead of always appending to the end. It is what lets space reclaimed by Node 9's vacuum actually get reused.

Visibility map — a companion file with a couple of bits per page, one of which marks pages where every tuple is visible to every transaction. Node 5's index-only scans and Node 9's vacuum both depend on it.

Sequential scan — reading every page of a relation in file order and examining every row.

Buffer — one page held in memory.

shared_buffers — the fixed block of memory, allocated at startup and shared by every backend process, in which Postgres caches pages. Default 128 MB.

Dirty page — a cached page that has been modified in memory but not yet written back to its file.

Eviction — removing a page from the cache to make room for another. Postgres chooses victims with a scheme called clock sweep, described below.

Operating system page cache — a second, separate cache of the same files, maintained by the operating system itself, filled automatically whenever any program reads a file. Postgres does not control it and cannot see into it.

effective_cache_size — a planner setting stating how much caching, from both caches combined, is likely to be available. It allocates no memory at all; it changes only estimates.

Physical correlation — how closely a column's sort order matches the physical order of rows in the file. A timestamp column on an append-only table has near-perfect correlation; a random UUID has none. It strongly affects how cheap an index scan turns out to be.

Row width — the average number of bytes a row occupies, including all headers and padding. Shown by EXPLAIN as width= on each plan node.

The history — why this exists at all

Why a page at all. Storage hardware has never let you read one byte. Disks have always transferred fixed-size units, and filesystems are built out of fixed-size blocks, so any program storing data on disk ends up choosing a chunk size and working in whole chunks. Once you are doing that, the chunk becomes the natural unit for everything else too: the unit you cache, the unit you write, the unit you count when estimating cost. Postgres picked 8192 bytes, and although it is a compile-time constant that can be changed, essentially nobody does, so you can treat it as universal.

Why 8192 specifically, and what the trade-off is. It is a compromise, and both directions have real costs. A larger page — 16 KB, 32 KB — means indexes with more keys per page and therefore fewer levels to descend, and fewer, larger I/O operations. But it also means that changing one small row forces a larger write, that more unrelated rows sit in the same cached unit and compete, and that the wasted space at the end of each page grows. A smaller page reverses all of that. 8192 sits close to typical filesystem block sizes, which keeps writes aligned with what the storage layer underneath is doing anyway. It is not a magic number; it is a defensible middle, chosen early and kept.

Why 1 GB segments. When Postgres's storage layer was written, many filesystems could not hold a file larger than 2 GB. Splitting relations into 1 GB pieces made the problem disappear, and the code was never changed because there was no reason to.

Why TOAST exists, and what life was like before it. A tuple cannot span pages — the line pointer scheme addresses a tuple by its offset within a page, so a row that did not fit in one would have no address. Before Postgres 7.1, released in 2001, that limitation was simply exposed to you: a row could not exceed about 8 KB, full stop. If you wanted to store an article, a document, or a large block of JSON, you could not. You split it into chunks yourself, in your application, and reassembled it on read.

TOAST solved this in 7.1 and is one of the more elegant pieces of the system, because it changed nothing about the tuple format: an oversized value is compressed, and if still too large is moved into a hidden side table in pieces, leaving a small fixed-size pointer in the original row. From SQL nothing is different — you select the column and get your megabyte back. The consequences for performance, described below, are entirely invisible until you go looking for them, which is exactly why they trip people up.

Why the companion maps arrived late. The free space map and visibility map both took their modern form in version 8.4 (2009). Before then, free space tracking was a fixed-size in-memory structure you had to size by hand, and getting it wrong meant vacuum silently failed to record reusable space and the table grew regardless. The visibility map was extended again in 9.6 to track frozen pages, which is what made the anti-wraparound vacuums of Node 9 skip work they had previously repeated. These are unglamorous parts of the system whose absence caused years of production pain, and they are a decent illustration that "Postgres is mature" means specifically that a great many problems like these have already been found and fixed.

The mechanism — traced

Inside a page. All 8192 bytes are accounted for, in four regions.

At the very start is the page header, 24 bytes. It holds a checksum, some flags, the page size and version, a field recording the write-ahead-log position of the last change to this page (which is Node 7's mechanism reaching in here), and crucially two offsets: pd_lower, the end of the line pointer array, and pd_upper, the start of the tuple data. The gap between those two is the page's free space.

Immediately after the header, growing downward into the page, is the line pointer array: 4 bytes per tuple, each recording where in this page that tuple starts, how long it is, and whether it is normal, dead, or redirected. Because everything outside the page refers to a tuple by its line pointer number rather than by a byte offset, the tuple can be shuffled within the page freely — and that is exactly what Node 9's vacuum does when it compacts a page.

From the far end, growing upward, are the tuples themselves. New rows are written at the bottom and the boundary creeps up.

Between the two is free space. When they meet, the page is full and the next insert goes elsewhere. (Index pages additionally use a small special region at the very end for structure such as sibling links; heap pages do not.)

Inside a tuple. The header is 23 bytes, padded up to 24, and none of it is your data:

  • t_xmin, 4 bytes — the transaction that created this version.
  • t_xmax, 4 bytes — the transaction that deleted or superseded it.
  • a 4-byte field holding the command id within the transaction.
  • t_ctid, 6 bytes — normally this tuple's own address, but repurposed to point at the newer version when one exists, which is how update chains are followed.
  • t_infomask2 and t_infomask, 2 bytes each — status bits, including the number of columns and cached conclusions about whether xmin and xmax committed.
  • t_hoff, 1 byte — where the actual data begins.

Then, if the row has any NULLs, the null bitmap; then padding to the first column's alignment; then your columns.

The number worth carrying away: about 28 bytes of pure overhead per row — 24 for the header, 4 for the line pointer. A table with a single boolean column costs roughly 29 bytes per row, not 1. This is why very narrow tables are far less efficient than they look, and why a join table of two bigints costs about 44 bytes a row rather than 16.

Alignment and column order. Postgres lays columns out in the order you declared them and inserts padding wherever the next column's alignment demands it. Consider two tables with identical columns:

CREATE TABLE bad  (a bool, b bigint, c bool, d bigint);
CREATE TABLE good (b bigint, d bigint, a bool, c bool);

In bad, the boolean takes 1 byte and the bigint that follows must start on an 8-byte boundary, so 7 bytes are wasted — twice. In good, the two 8-byte values sit together and the two booleans pack side by side at the end. Same data, and bad is 16 bytes per row larger. At ten thousand rows this is meaningless. At a billion rows it is 16 GB of disk, cache and I/O bought for nothing.

The working rule is to declare fixed-width columns largest first, then smaller fixed-width ones, then variable-length columns, then anything usually NULL. Do not contort a schema for this — readability of a table definition is worth real money too — but on your largest table it is free to get right at creation time, and expensive to fix later because changing column order requires rebuilding the table.

TOAST, step by step. When a row is about to be written, Postgres checks its total size. If it exceeds roughly 2000 bytes — chosen so that at least four rows fit per page — it starts working on the largest variable-length columns, in order:

First it compresses them, if their storage strategy permits. If the row now fits, it stops. If not, it moves the largest values out entirely: the value is cut into chunks of just under 2000 bytes, each chunk is written as a row in a hidden side table (named pg_toast.pg_toast_<oid>, one per table that needs one, with its own index), and an 18-byte pointer replaces the value in the original row.

Each column has a storage strategy controlling this, settable with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STORAGE ...: EXTENDED (compress then move out) is the default for variable-length types; EXTERNAL moves out without compressing, which makes substring operations on the value much faster because it need not be decompressed whole; MAIN compresses but avoids moving out if it can; PLAIN does neither and is the only option for fixed-width types.

The consequence that actually matters is this. A row with a large TOASTed column is small in the heap — 18 bytes for that column. Reading the row without selecting that column touches only the heap. Selecting the column means following the pointer, reading several rows from the TOAST table through its index, and decompressing. So on a table with one large column, SELECT * can be an order of magnitude more expensive than SELECT id, name, and nothing in the query text hints at it. This is the concrete, mechanical version of "don't use SELECT *", and it is far more persuasive than the usual style argument.

The sequential scan. With nothing but a heap, answering WHERE email = 'x' means reading page 0, checking every row, reading page 1, and so on to the end. Its cost is exactly the page count. A 50 GB table is about 6.5 million pages, and if every request does that, the work discarded is essentially all of it.

It is worth being clear that a sequential scan is not a bad thing. It is one long streaming read, which storage hardware handles better than scattered access, and for a small table, or for a query matching a large fraction of a big one, it is genuinely the fastest available strategy. The planner in Node 6 chooses it deliberately far more often than people expect, and it is usually right.

The buffer cache, and the second cache underneath it. Postgres does not read files directly on every access. At startup it allocates shared_buffers as an array of 8 KB slots shared by every backend, and a page is read from disk into a slot the first time it is wanted. When all slots are full, one must be evicted, and Postgres chooses using a clock sweep: each buffer has a small usage counter, incremented when accessed; a pointer sweeps round the array, decrementing counters as it passes and evicting the first buffer whose counter has reached zero. The effect is that frequently used pages survive and rarely used ones do not, without the cost of maintaining an exact ordering.

One refinement is worth knowing because it explains a behaviour people find surprising: a large sequential scan does not get to evict the whole cache. Postgres gives such scans a small ring buffer — a few hundred kilobytes reused in a circle — so that one report scanning a huge table cannot flush every hot page belonging to everyone else. Without it, a nightly analytics query would leave the database cold every morning.

Underneath all of that, the operating system maintains its own cache of the same files, filled whenever any program reads them. So a page missing from shared_buffers is frequently still in memory and comes back very fast, which is why Postgres's cache hit ratio understates how much is really cached. This double caching is unusual — Oracle and MySQL's InnoDB conventionally take a very large share of memory for their own buffer pool and bypass the OS cache — and it is the reason for two pieces of standard advice that otherwise look contradictory. Set shared_buffers to about 25% of RAM, not 80%, because the rest is doing useful work in the other cache and duplicating everything twice would waste it. And set effective_cache_size to 50–75% of RAM, because that setting allocates nothing at all — it exists purely to tell the planner how much caching to assume, which changes how expensive it thinks repeated index access will be, and therefore changes plans without changing a single allocation.

Seeing all of it. The definitive tool is the pageinspect extension, and it takes one command to install:

CREATE EXTENSION pageinspect;

-- the page header of the first page
SELECT * FROM page_header(get_raw_page('bookings', 0));

-- every line pointer and tuple header on that page
SELECT lp, lp_off, lp_len, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid
FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('bookings', 0));

That second query prints, for one page of your own table, exactly the structures described above: the line pointers with their offsets and lengths, and each tuple's xmin, xmax and ctid. Run it once and the layout stops being a diagram. It is also the single best way to see Node 8 and Node 9 happening — update a row and watch a second tuple appear on the page with the first one's xmax now set.

The everyday functions are simpler. pg_relation_size('bookings') gives the heap alone; pg_indexes_size the indexes; pg_table_size the heap plus TOAST; pg_total_relation_size everything. Wrap any of them in pg_size_pretty for human-readable output. pg_column_size(value) reports the stored size of a single value including compression, so comparing it against octet_length shows you what TOAST compression actually achieved. And relpages and reltuples in pg_class hold the planner's idea of the page and row counts — estimates, refreshed by ANALYZE, not live values.

In your project

Stage 4 of slotline is where this node stops being reading. The stage's stated purpose is volume — a seeder that fills the database to ten thousand rows or ten million, with deliberate skew — and the first honest EXPLAIN. But before the plans, the spec has you look at the physical reality of what you just built, and now you know what you are looking at.

Four investigations, each of which takes minutes:

Confirm the arithmetic. Read relpages from pg_class for bookings, multiply by 8192, and compare against the actual file size at the path you found in Node 1. They should match. That single check collapses the distance between "a table is a bag of rows" and "a table is a file of 8 KB pages" permanently.

Open a page. Install pageinspect and run heap_page_items on page 0. You will see your own rows as line pointers and headers. Note the t_xmin values — they are the transaction ids from your seeder, and in Stage 3 you already read those same fields on the duplicate bookings your concurrency test produced. This is the same structure viewed from underneath.

Measure TOAST. The notes column on bookings is your candidate. Seed some rows with a paragraph and some with several kilobytes, then compare pg_column_size(notes) against octet_length(notes) to see compression working, check whether a TOAST table was created with SELECT reltoastrelid FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'bookings', and time SELECT * against SELECT id, resource_id, during over the whole table with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). The buffer counts will differ far more than the row counts do, and that measurement is a good first entry for docs/plans/.

Prove the column-order effect. Create two tables with identical columns in the two orders shown above, seed a million rows into each from the same source, and compare pg_relation_size. It is a five-minute experiment producing a number you will never forget, and it is exactly the kind of thing that is far more convincing to describe in an interview than to assert.

One forward pointer: the fillfactor defined in this node does nothing yet. It becomes load-bearing in Stage 10, where update churn produces bloat, because free space on a page is what allows Node 8's HOT updates to avoid touching indexes at all.

In qbank

qbank stores raw model responses, and that is a textbook TOAST case: a column that is occasionally kilobytes, on rows you list and filter constantly without needing it. Two things follow, and both are checkable in an afternoon.

First, find out whether your list endpoints select that column. Drizzle's db.select().from(table) with no argument selects every column, which is the ORM's default and is exactly the SELECT * the mechanism above makes expensive. Passing an explicit column object to select() is the fix, and the difference will be visible in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) as a large drop in buffers read rather than in rows returned.

Second, look at the sizes: pg_total_relation_size against pg_relation_size on your largest table tells you how much of it is indexes and TOAST rather than heap, and if the TOAST table dominates, that is a strong argument for keeping the raw payload in a separate table joined only when needed — which costs one join on the rare path and takes the weight off every common one.

Neither of these is knowledge an ORM was ever going to give you. They are visible only from underneath, which is the point of this node.

What an interviewer does with this

"How does Postgres actually store a row?" A senior-flavoured question and a strong opportunity, because most candidates cannot answer it at all. Tables are heaps of 8 KB pages; each page has a header, a line pointer array growing down, tuples growing up, and free space between; each tuple carries a 23-byte header of transaction bookkeeping before any of your data, so a row costs about 28 bytes before its first column. Mentioning that the header is where MVCC lives connects it forward and shows the model is joined up.

"Why is SELECT * bad?" The weak answer is "you fetch data you don't need" or "it breaks when columns change". Those are true and small. The strong answer is TOAST: a large value is stored out of line, so selecting a column you do not need can turn a single heap read into a heap read plus an index lookup plus several TOAST chunk reads plus decompression — per row. Then add that SELECT * also prevents index-only scans, which is Node 5.

"What is TOAST?" A row cannot span a page, so a value pushing a row past about 2 KB is compressed and, if still too large, split into chunks in a hidden side table with an 18-byte pointer left behind. Transparent to SQL. Then the history, which lands well: before version 7.1 there was no TOAST and a row simply could not exceed 8 KB, so applications chunked large values by hand.

"Why is my table so much bigger than my data?" Four causes, and being able to list them in order is the answer: per-row overhead of about 28 bytes, which dominates on narrow tables; alignment padding from column order; indexes, which are counted by pg_total_relation_size but not by pg_relation_size; and dead tuples from Node 9, which is usually the real answer on a table that has been in production a while.

"What is shared_buffers and how large should it be?" Postgres's own page cache, shared by all backends, allocated at startup, evicted by clock sweep. About 25% of RAM — and the reason is the good part: the operating system caches the same files independently, so allocating most of memory to Postgres would cache everything twice. Then the follow-up you can pre-empt: effective_cache_size allocates nothing and describes the combined caching to the planner, which changes plans without changing memory.

"Does column order matter?" Usually asked as a trick, and the answer is yes, for storage, because of alignment padding — with the honest qualifier that it is irrelevant below a few million rows and worth attending to only on your largest tables. Having actually measured it is what makes the answer sound like experience rather than trivia.
